item.title: Moving from Jekyll to Hugo
item.description:
Almost ten years ago, I moved from WordPress to Jekyll. It felt like time for another change, so I have now moved the site to Hugo. There was no particular need for it, build times weren't too bad, but it is nice to see how much faster Hugo is in building my website.

The migration is complete, and I have tried to make sure everything still works as intended. Let me know if something did break!

item.title: I've joined the editorial board of Journal of Noncommutative Geometry
item.description:
I am pleased and honoured to announce that I have joined the editorial board of Journal of Noncommutative Geometry. The word algebraic is implicit in its name, as the journal serves both the NCG and NCAG communities.

Please submit your interesting and high-quality papers on noncommutative algebraic geometry, so that the journal can continue its role as a leading journal in this particular niche!

item.title: Updated contact information
item.description:
Today is my first day (physically) at Utrecht University.

From now on, please get in touch using p.belmans@uu.nl. My former University of Luxembourg address is no longer active: it is their policy to not have a grace period or forwarding set up, which is pretty inconvenient for any academic. I am sorry for the inconvenience this will cause...

If you find any out-of-date contact information, please let me know!

item.title: Moving to Utrecht University
item.description:
I am really excited to share here the news that I will be moving to Utrecht University, starting from January 1. I am also very much looking forward to integrating in the vibrant Dutch algebraic geometry community, which I participated in as an outsider over the past 10+ years. I will at the same time miss working in Luxembourg.

Today it was also announced that I am the recipient of a Vidi grant, from the NWO, for a project focusing on noncommutative algebraic geometry. I thank the NWO for the confidence they have in me, and I'm looking forward to all of the exciting noncommutative algebraic geometry I will be working on!

item.title: I've joined the editorial board of Experimental Mathematics
item.description:
This has been on the website for a few months now, but I have joined the editorial board for Experimental Mathematics, following the "reboot" led by Al Kasprzyk.

Please submit your interesting and high-quality experimental papers, so that the journal can continue its role as a leading journal in this particular niche!

item.title: Starting at the University of Luxembourg
item.description: Monday was my first day at the University of Luxembourg. This means a new email address to reach me (pieter.belmans@uni.lu).

item.title: Ida Belmans
item.description:
Here's an important real-life update: last week our daughter Ida was born. All is well with her, and with the two (slightly sleep-deprived) people who do their best to keep her in good health.

There will be slightly less blog activity (and programming in particular), but the fortnightly links will return this Sunday. Given how little space is otherwise dedicated to personal updates on this blog I think I'll just leave it at this :).

item.title: Moving to the University of Luxembourg
item.description:
I am very excited to share the news that I'll be starting as an assistant professor at the University of Luxembourg this summer. I'm really looking forward to start!

Not entirely unrelated to the message above the fold, I'd like to advertise:

  • this postdoc position, associated to Sarah Scherotzke.
  • these 3 PhD positions, which can be taken up with 5 of my future colleagues.

Especially for the postdoc position: in case you wish to work on topics that Sarah Scherotzke is interested in, it could be useful to know that I'll be starting there too, given the overlap between our research interests.

item.title: Moving to the University of Bonn
item.description:
A quick update: starting April 1, I will move to the University of Bonn. You can already start emailing me at pbelmans@math.uni-bonn.de.

Also, you might have noticed a lack of blog posts in the past weeks, which can be explained by me being on vacation.

item.title: Starting my postdoc
item.description: A quick update: This week I have started my postdoc at the Max Planck Institute for Mathematics in Bonn. Feel free to come and say hi in office 402.

item.title: Moving from WordPress to Jekyll
item.description: My first post was little over six years ago, and it has become time to move my weblog from WordPress to Jekyll, integrating it with my personal webpage. I have become a great fan of Jekyll, and after so many years I started to dislike the fact that I had two completely disjoint websites: one for blogging, and the other acting more like my business card. This is no longer the case now.

item.title: Stacks project website bug fixing
item.description:
Today I decided to spend some time improving the website for the Stacks project, fixing bugs and implementing some small improvements. I grouped the issues in the GitHub issue tracker that I wanted to address. Here are two highlights, not because the bugfix was interesting, but because you might learn something about how to use the website.

  • the search now works better with quotes: If you want to learn about quasicoherent sheaves in the Stacks project, you should first of all know that the spelling quasi-coherent is used. Then it is important to know that if you want to use the search function to find results about quasi-coherent sheaves, you should enclose it with quotes. item.title: More 'Infinite Jest' web goodies
item.description:
My love for David Foster Wallace's Infinite Jest has been expressed before, where I linked to the wonderful tumblr Poor Yorick Entertainment. Now there is something new: an involved art project by William Beutler based on Infinite Jest. There is:

  • Infinite Atlas which maps all locations used in the book on Google Maps;
  • Infinite Boston which contains a really thorough discussion of locations in Infinite Jest, including photographs!
  • Infinite Shop where you can buy Infinite Jest related stuff if you feel like supporting the project.

With all this interesting stuff I feel a reread coming up.

item.title: Personal update
item.description:
Not that this blog is considered to be the medium for all my personal tidbits, but to sketch a little context for what I might be blogging about in the upcoming year I think it is appropriate to explain my current whereabouts and plans.

I will be doing the second year of the master in mathematics at Ecole Polytechnique and Université Paris-Sud XI, specializing in algebraic geometry and number theory. So this means my blog might get a little more focus where mathematics is concerned. And probably I will be creating all kinds of LaTeX templates tailored to my current home universities :).

item.title: A visual exploration of the filmography of James O. Incandenza and the world of David Foster Wallace's "Infinite Jest."
item.description:
Because that's what it is.

When reading Infinite Jest I always wondered whether someone would ever make all the fake cultural references real. This thought occurred to me several times, when imaginary fiction or movies were mentioned in a book. But Wallace's universe in Infinite Jest is so immensely littered with non-existing movie plots it really screams for elaboration. Which is now being done, hurray!

In case you haven't read Infinite Jest and you are looking for a tip for your summer reading: please consider it. It is amazing.

item.title: Math joke
item.description:
A mathematician's view on true love:

I don't believe in true love. But I do believe in local optima and the social undesirability of a shotgun hill climbing approach.

item.title: Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, or 3 math novels
item.description: Let's start at the beginning. I was reading Don DeLillo's Ratner's Star. As a great fan of DeLillo I was excited to read this one as it is about a mathematician in a sci-fi setting. That sounds like 2 great things combined. Unfortunately, this is either a bad novel or I don't understand it. But surely it is a false dichotomy! Which is my favourite logical fallacy by the way.

item.title: Ska comics
item.description: Such a silly but amazing idea: Left-Handed Toons. I've been following them for a while now and they vary from absolutely horrendous to brilliant. Maybe brilliant in the I-want-to-kick-myself-in-the-head way, but brilliant. As I consider myself expert of the web comics (having built a web comic aggregator for a database course once, forcing me to read through feeds and feeds of comics to check everything (yeah right, I was just procrastinating)) I should spread the word about this one.

item.title: Photographs of the Paris metro
item.description: As I opened this blog with a (rather silly) description of my trip to Paris, almost 4 months ago, I guess this is a nice sequel to it. Some urban photographers have taken pictures in the unused parts of the Paris metro, see Demolition of the Paris Metro. I don't know what it is, but urban photography is such an interesting concept. I don't know whether it is cheap and easy as a subject or not, but I like it. My personal favourite for sightseeing (I'm no photographer) is the unused canal in a village nearby and any excavation for a large building. Please don't laugh at me when you see me drooling over an excavation (which I feel is a lousy translation for the Dutch 'bouwput' which literally translates to 'building pit', any suggestions?).

item.title: This is how I feel nowadays
item.description:
The web comic Spided Math has written my biography.

By the way, I've been typing the course notes for my Commutative algebra course. And the draft is finished now! Hurray!

item.title: A mathematical joke
item.description:
Why did Benjamin, son of Jacob, join the Tea Party movement? Because Jacobson's radical.

Hopefully not the best math joke around.

item.title: Paris
item.description:
Apparently, Paris:

  • provides its inhabitants with an amazing metro network, the people using it are very polite too;
  • is the most beige city I ever hope to see, beautiful but beige in every view;
  • contains the wonderful Cité de la Musique with the astounding Musée de la Musique, I hope they will expand their collection (after the pop music extension already that's in the make) with a section devoted to tuning experiments as I'd love to see real life quarter-tone pianos etc. and seeing the UPIC system on which Xenakis composed Mycènes Alpha was a wonderful thing to do apart from the amazing guitar and variants thereupon collection;
  • has other characteristics apart from the ones listed above.

Too bad Wordpress.com does not let me provide a lang or xml:lang attribute on the links.

item.title: Introduction
item.description:
Not that I'm intending to blog regularly, but at least there is a completely set-up space to do so in case the urge kicks in. When the actual blogging will start, it will be featuring stuff on (computational or algorithmic) composition and ramblings on both computer science and mathematics.

For now, please enjoy yourself reading something more interesting. I'd suggest Pafko at the Wall from Don DeLillo.
